claims.text: Adding aluminum to a refractory high-entropy alloy can improve its high-temperature oxidation resistance.
A few atomic percent of aluminum is sufficient to produce the proposed oxidation-resistance improvement.
Aluminum addition promotes formation of a continuous oxide scale.
The continuous oxide scale formed by the aluminum-modified refractory alloy is specifically alumina (Al2O3).
The alumina scale is slow-growing and adherent.
Aluminum has a high affinity for oxygen and preferentially oxidizes during high-temperature exposure.
Aluminum oxidation produces a dense, protective Al2O3 layer.
The protective oxide layer impedes further oxygen transport and oxidation of the underlying alloy.
Relative to the untreated alloy, the aluminum-modified alloy will have a significantly lower oxidation rate and oxide weight gain.
The aluminum-modified alloy will form a more stable oxide scale than the untreated alloy.
Improved oxidation resistance will enhance the alloy's structural integrity under extreme-temperature conditions.
The untreated refractory high-entropy alloy undergoes rapid oxidation and oxide-scale degradation under the specified conditions.
The intervention will be beneficial at 1200–1300 °C in air or pure oxygen over approximately 100 hours.
At lower temperatures or in less oxidizing atmospheres, protective-alumina formation kinetics may differ.
Aluminum addition can cause brittle intermetallic formation and reduce the mechanical properties of refractory high-entropy alloys.

contradictions.description: The mediator is described as a slow-growing alumina scale, whereas the falsification rule treats a thicker alumina scale as a favorable indicator. Greater thickness is not clearly consistent with slow growth and may instead indicate more extensive oxidation.
